questions.q: Who founded the Shunga dynasty, and in what year did he seize power from the last Mauryan ruler?
questions.a: Pushyamitra Shunga, a Brahmin commander-in-chief (senapati), founded the Shunga dynasty c. 185 BCE by assassinating the last Mauryan ruler Brihadratha during a military parade. A wrong answer (e.g., "Ashoka's son" or "321 BCE") reveals confusion between Mauryan foundation and Shunga usurpation, and inability to distinguish between Kshatriya Mauryas and Brahmin Shungas — a critical ideological shift.

questions.q: Why did the Shungas, despite being Brahmin rulers who allegedly persecuted Buddhists, sponsor additions to the Buddhist stupa at Sanchi?
questions.a: The Shungas expanded the Sanchi stupa (railings, gateways) to integrate themselves into the existing sacred landscape and win legitimacy among local populations; patronage was political, not purely religious. A wrong answer ("they were Buddhist" or "they destroyed all stupas") reveals a binary misconception: students assume Brahmin rulers = anti-Buddhist, missing the pragmatic politics of patronage seen in Satavahana and later Gupta practice.

questions.q: The Satavahana king Gautamiputra Satakarni's Nashik inscription (by his mother Gautami Balashri) claims he "destroyed the pride of the Kshatriyas" and "restored the four-fold varna order." How does this claim function as political legitimation in the post-Mauryan Deccan?
questions.a: The inscription positions Gautamiputra as a Brahmanical restorer of dharma after a period of "mleccha" (foreign) and mixed-varna rule (Shakas), aligning him with Puranic ideals to legitimize his lineage (claimed Brahmin gotra) and authority over feudatories. A wrong answer focusing only on military victory misses the ideological work: the inscription uses varna rhetoric to convert military success into moral authority — a pattern repeated in Gupta prashastis.

questions.q: Compare the Shunga and Satavahana strategies for legitimizing rule. Identify two similarities and two differences in their use of religion, lineage, and geography.
questions.a: Similarities: Both claimed Brahmin status (Shungas by birth, Satavahanas by gotra) and patronized Buddhist monuments (Sanchi, Amaravati) for popular legitimacy. Differences: Shungas ruled from the former Mauryan heartland (Pataliputra) and emphasized Vedic sacrifices (ashvamedha); Satavahanas ruled the Deccan, controlled Dakshinapatha trade, used matronymics (Gautamiputra, Vashishthiputra) to highlight royal women's status, and issued bilingual coins (Prakrit + Greek) for cross-cultural trade. A wrong answer listing only "one was north, one south" misses the comparative analysis of legitimation tools.

questions.q: Evaluate the historian's claim: "The Kanva dynasty (c. 73–28 BCE) was a mere footnote between the Shungas and Satavahanas." Use evidence from inscriptions and Puranas to defend or critique this view.
questions.a: Critique: The Kanvas (four kings, 45 years) were brief but significant — they continued Shunga administrative structures, maintained Brahmanical orthodoxy, and their overthrow by the Satavahanas (per Puranas) marks the Deccan's definitive political rise. Calling them a "footnote" reflects north-centric bias; the Kanva-Satavahana transition shows how Deccan powers absorbed northern legitimation models. A wrong answer agreeing uncritically reveals reliance on textbook summaries without engaging Puranic/epigraphic evidence of continuity.

questions.q: Construct a timeline (185 BCE–250 CE) showing the sequential and overlapping rules of the Shungas, Kanvas, and Satavahanas, marking: (a) key rulers, (b) major inscriptions/coins, (c) shifts in trade route control (Uttarapatha vs. Dakshinapatha).
questions.a: A strong answer shows: 185 BCE – Pushyamitra Shunga; c. 150 BCE – Sanchi stupa expansion; 73 BCE – Vasudeva Kanva; 28 BCE – Satavahana rise (Simuka); 1st century CE – Gautamiputra Satakarni (Nashik inscription, Shaka defeat); 2nd century CE – Vashishthiputra Pulumavi (Amaravati patronage, Roman trade coins); c. 250 CE – Satavahana decline. Overlap: Satavahanas begin during late Kanva period. A poor answer lists dates without linking to trade routes or inscriptional evidence, treating dynasties as isolated blocks.
